**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

A thousand words. A thousand thoughts, a thousand breaths, a thousand moments stretched thin like the last light of a dying star.

I write to capture the fragments before they slip away—before the coffee cools, before the bookmark falls, before the thought dissolves into the hum of the refrigerator. Words are the only thing I know how to hold onto, the only currency that doesn’t rust or fade.

Some days, the words come easy. Like rain on a tin roof, loud and insistent, demanding to be heard. Other days, the page stays blank, a cemetery of unsaid things. A thousand words could be a poem, could be a scream into the void, could be a love letter to a stranger.

I’ve written to people I’ll never meet—scrawled on napkins, scribbled in margins, whispered to the empty sky. Words are bridges, but sometimes they’re also walls. They can free you or imprison you, depending on who’s holding the pen.

What do I write when I have a thousand words? The truth? A lie? A half-truth twisted into something beautiful? A thousand words could be a confession, an apology, a myth. Or it could just be noise.

But noise has power too. It says: *I was here.* Even if no one listens.

So here I am. Writing. Always writing.
